Using a data sample of $3.0\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector at $\sqrt{s}=8\,\mathrm{TeV}$, the study searches for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays. The analysis yields a significance of $3.8\,\sigma$ for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ transition and reports the first observation of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$. The branching fractions are determined to be $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S)=(1.50^{+0.22}_{-0.19}\pm0.04\pm0.04)\times10^{-2}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S)=(0.85^{+0.13}_{-0.11}\pm0.04\pm0.03)\times10^{-2}$, where the uncertainties are attributed to statistical precision, systematic effects, and the reliance on the $\mathcal{B}(B^0\to\bar{D}^0\pi^0)=(3.91\pm0.15)\times10^{-2}$ branching fraction. These results are compared with predictions derived from both theoretical models and experimental measurements.

This paper addresses the challenge of constructing the submodule lattice for multiplicity-free modules associated with classical Lie algebras, using a novel algorithm that leverages the multiplicity vector and the collection of submodule multiplicity vectors. We demonstrate the application of this algorithm to specific modules and explore its potential for resolving open problems in this domain. Additionally, we introduce a heuristic designed to generate the submodule lattice for arbitrary modules. Finally, we provide a complete description of the lattice for the module $V(2\omega_1+\omega_2)$ of $\mathfrak{sl}_5$, which corresponds to the Weyl module $\Delta(2\omega_1+\omega_2)$ of type $A_4$ over a suitable Lie algebra of classical type. As a byproduct of our analysis, we present a collection of tables detailing the submodule lattice for $V(2\omega_1+\omega_2)$ across various Lie algebras of classical type. These tables serve as a valuable resource for future investigations into the multiplicities of extremal weights within submodules of fundamental representations of Lie algebras of classical type. Ultimately, our work offers a practical method for generating submodule lattices from the multiplicities of highest weights, a feature that could prove beneficial in other areas of research. This study examines biharmonic hypersurfaces equipped with recurring curvature tensors within Euclidean space. We establish that a biharmonic hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with the Ricci operator recurring along a specific direction is necessarily minimal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a biharmonic hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ where the Riemannian curvature tensor is recurring must be an open product of a sphere and a Euclidean space. Finally, we prove that if the square of the Riemannian curvature tensor is recurring, the hypersurface must be a product of a sphere and a Euclidean space. These findings generalize earlier results by B.Y. Chen and others. Additionally, we show that a biharmonic hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with the square of the Ricci tensor recurring is either minimal or a specific type of cylinder over a sphere. As a consequence, we derive a generalized characterization of the product of a sphere and a Euclidean space when the square of the Riemannian curvature tensor is $\mathcal{Q}_\mathcal{R}$-recurrent.

A family of graphs is termed $p/q$-identifiable if, for any two distinct edges $e$ and $f$, the subgraph obtained by deleting $e$ is isomorphic to the subgraph resulting from deleting $q(e)$ from $f$, where $q$ represents a function mapping edges to their endpoints. This concept extends to graphs, offering a generalization of the identifiable family of graphs. We demonstrate that the family of trees which are $p/q$-identifiable constitutes a finite collection. Furthermore, we establish that the line graph of a complete graph $K_n$ is $p/q$-identifiable if and only if $n \leq 4$. Additionally, we prove that for any graph $G$, the family of its subgraphs which are $p/q$-identifiable is itself identifiable. Finally, we show that if $G$ is a $p/q$-identifiable graph with at least three edges, then $G$ must be connected. These findings generalize results previously reported in [1] and [2]. Our proofs rely on the concept of walks, which are sequences of edges where consecutive edges share a common vertex. We also introduce the notion of a walk's height, defined as the maximum distance between any pair of its vertices. The paper begins by defining walks and height, followed by the introduction of identifiable graphs and the $p/q$-identifiable property. It concludes with the proof of our primary theorem.

This study presents the initial measurement of the differential decay rate for the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ process with respect to the hadron recoil variable $w$. The analysis utilizes a data sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $3.0\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector at $\sqrt{s}=8\,\mathrm{TeV}$. The differential decay rate is extracted by fitting the invariant mass distribution of the $B_s^0$ candidate in the signal region, utilizing a model derived from the weighted product of the invariant mass distributions of the $D_s^{*-}$, $\mu^{+}$, and $B_s^0$ candidates. The form factor is parameterized using the ZW model, which aligns with the results obtained from the fit. The determined differential decay rate at $w=0$ is $(1.01\pm 0.07(\mathrm{stat.})\pm 0.07(\mathrm{syst.}))\times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{fs}^{-1}$. Furthermore, the differential decay rate across the full range of $w$ is modeled via a linear combination of Legendre polynomials, yielding a coefficient of $-0.01\pm 0.01(\mathrm{stat.})\pm 0.01(\mathrm{syst.})$ for the $P_2(w)$ term. These findings are consistent with expectations from both the ZW and BCL parameterizations. Ultimately, the form of the differential decay rate is visualized, and the extracted coefficients are compared against predictions from various theoretical models.

When an adhesive strip is pulled from a surface, it generates a sequence of snapping sounds known as stick-slip crackling. This phenomenon was investigated using a 10 cm wide strip of Sellotape removed from a glass pane at speeds ranging from 0.001 to 1 cm/s. The resulting acoustic emission signal was analyzed via wavelet transform to extract local characteristics, which were then sorted into distinct events based on their local features. These events were subsequently grouped into discrete events (DEs) by identifying transitions between them. The findings indicate that the local characteristics of these events are independent of the peeling velocity, and that the distribution of DE sizes aligns with a power law. This distribution exhibits a cutoff at larger sizes that scales linearly with the peeling speed, suggesting a universal distribution of discrete events across different speeds. These results support the hypothesis that the size distribution of discrete events follows a power law, implying that the stick-slip crackling arises from an avalanche process governed by an underlying concealed arrangement. This arrangement is likely the result of the superposition of multiple spatially localized modes of instability. The local characteristics of these events were compared with the local stress concentration at the tip of a crack, offering insights into the nature of the events and their associated local deformation. Furthermore, the local characteristics of events occurring at the same time were examined to determine if they share common origins. The analysis of the evolution of local characteristics over time supports the existence of a sequence of events originating from a single source, a behavior analogous to the branching observed in earthquake aftershocks. This sequence of events from a single source was utilized to reconstruct the spatial distribution of events, revealing a spatially organized pattern of discrete events. This organization is attributed to the anisotropic nature of the events, which is linked to the directionality of stress concentration at the crack tip. Additionally, the local characteristics of events were compared with the local deformation observed at the tape's surface through stroboscopic imaging. This comparison provides evidence that the local characteristics of the discrete events correspond to the local deformation of the tape, thereby connecting acoustic emissions with surface deformations. Ultimately, the local characteristics of these events were related to the local deformation of the tape, and the spatial distribution of events was compared with the global deformation of the tape. Kurt Menger introduced the concept of an abstract angle function and investigated its properties within metric spaces in 1931. He defined axioms for an abstract angle function and demonstrated that, when combined with axioms for a metric, these could yield an axiomatic system for Hilbert geometry. Additionally, he explored the connection between an abstract angle function and ordered triples of points known as turns. In 1932, Menger posed two questions concerning the equivalence of axioms for the angle function and those for turns. Although these issues were set aside, they resurfaced in 1998 when Euclidean geometry was axiomatized using an angle function; there, it was observed that the standard axioms for the Euclidean angle function did not guarantee the existence of a global coordinate system, a problem resolved by introducing a new axiom. In this work, we revisit the concept of an abstract angle function, offering a comprehensive set of axioms for an angle function in metric spaces. We examine the relationship between axioms for the angle function and those for turns, proving the equivalence of axiom sets for the angle function with those for turns plus a condition ensuring the metric satisfies the triangle equality. Furthermore, we provide a complete axiomatization of Euclidean geometry based on a metric and an abstract angle function. Our approach involves defining an abstract Euclidean distance function and establishing its equivalence to the original metric, followed by applying Monge's theorem from 1830 to construct Cartesian coordinates. Along the way, we clarify the historical development of this concept and its role in the axiomatization of Euclidean geometry. Finally, we apply our findings to Hilbert geometry, deriving an axiomatization of Hilbert geometry from an abstract metric and an angle function, and illustrating how to construct the corresponding geodesics.

Smoothing techniques are frequently employed to address data sparsity in neural network training for natural language processing and related domains. However, applying smoothing to point cloud data is challenging due to the data's inherent sparsity and high dimensionality. Furthermore, standard smoothing methods often fail to deliver significant performance gains. This work introduces a transformation-dependent smoothing approach designed to mitigate data sparsity in point cloud datasets. We demonstrate that the optimal smoothing factor varies based on the specific transformation being learned. Extensive experiments conducted on three standard point cloud datasets show that our transformation-dependent smoothing method outperforms conventional smoothing strategies and other state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence supporting the claim that our method effectively alleviates data sparsity. The source code is available at https://github.com/Point-TPC/Point-TPC.

This paper introduces a geometric approach to verifying the correctness of automated reasoning systems when used for program examinations. The core concept involves defining a geometric principle for program correctness and demonstrating its application to an automated verification system for a course assessment. The findings indicate that this geometric principle can be utilized to establish the correctness of an automated reasoning system for a specific program examination. Furthermore, this principle can be extended to verify the end-to-end correctness of an automated reasoning system for a program examination, including both the testing-based correctness of the system's strategies and the validity of the selected correct solutions. Finally, this geometric principle offers a novel, non-testing-based method for verifying the correctness of strategies within an automated reasoning system during a program examination. The concept of this geometric principle and its associated verification method are applicable to any combination of a program and its correctness proof, whether for an automated reasoning system in a course assessment or for other programs and their verified correctness proofs.

This paper offers a concise proof of the existence of $\mathscr{L}$-distinguished Serre weights for $\GL_2$, which are now termed "clear" distinguished weights. The proof relies on constructing explicit lifting operators via Kummer theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these weight characters are necessary for the existence of $p$-adic families of distinguished lifting within the ordinary context. Additionally, we establish that the lifting operators introduced here are optimal in the sense of Sen rank. Finally, we provide an explicit construction of these operators for the case where $p=2$.

This study introduces a novel method for determining the exact harmonic contour required for effective linearized self-sensing composite strategies. The approach combines electrical impedance tomography (an inversion technique) with evolutionary algorithms to extract the true nonlinear relationship between stress and electrical conductivity. Once established, this exact contour serves as the foundation for various linearized self-sensing strategies. The paper evaluates multiple linearized methods, including the affine, global slope, and local slope approaches, against the exact nonlinear model across different sensor types, geometries, and operating ranges. Results indicate that the exact harmonic contour yields a significant performance boost for local slope-based strategies, enabling them to surpass the accuracy of the exact nonlinear model in specific scenarios. Furthermore, the exact harmonic contour can facilitate other future self-sensing strategies. The proposed inversion-based method for deriving the exact stress-conductivity contour is broadly applicable to any self-sensing composite, regardless of filler type, matrix composition, or geometry. Additionally, the exact harmonic contour can support other inversion techniques, such as electrical impedance tomography itself, to reconstruct spatial conductivity fields from boundary measurements. The described methods are demonstrated using a widely adopted conductive rubber composite, but they are universally applicable to all self-sensing composites.

This study examines geometric concepts within the tensor framework of Euclidean spaces, with a specific focus on the area and volume of hyperspheres. We demonstrate that the area of an $n$-sphere and the volume of an $n$-ball can be expressed as contravariant tensor quantities. These expressions rely on the Euclidean metric tensor and a newly defined tensor, termed the generalized Levi-Civita tensor. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the generalized Levi-Civita tensor and the standard Levi-Civita tensor. Finally, we derive the formula for the area of an $n$-sphere defined by a hypersurface. This derivation utilizes the generalized Levi-Civita tensor, the Euclidean metric tensor, and a tensor representing the normal vector to the hypersurface. The resulting expression for the hypersphere's area is shown to be equivalent to the previously established formula. These findings offer a geometric perspective on the Euclidean space tensor representation and may find utility in theoretical physics. The discussion herein is confined to Euclidean spaces.

We demonstrate that a collection of subgroups $H_1, \ldots, H_k$ of a right-angled Artin group $A(\Gamma)$ constitutes a division if and only if the associated graph $\Gamma(H)$, constructed from the commutation relations among generators of $H_i$ within $A(\Gamma)$, is a subgraph of $\Gamma$ and the quotient graph $\Gamma(H)/H_i$ is a tree for each $i=1,\ldots,k$. Furthermore, we establish that a division of $A(\Gamma)$ into subgroups $H_1, \ldots, H_k$ admits a graph of spaces decomposition where $H_i$ stabilizes an $F$-space $X_i$ for each $i$, and the fundamental group of the linking graph of spaces of $X_i$ and $X_j$ is isomorphic to $[H_i,H_j]$. Finally, we prove that $A(\Gamma)$ decomposes as the free product of these $F$-spaces amalgamated over the commutator subgroups $[H_i,H_j]$. As a consequence, we derive a criterion for the hyperbolicity of such decompositions. Additionally, we show that $A(\Gamma)$ does not admit a non-trivial splitting as an HNN extension over a cyclic subgroup, nor as a graph of spaces where edge groups are cyclic and vertex spaces are hyperbolic, unless $\Gamma$ is a join graph. These findings yield new results regarding the acyclicity of Roller boundaries and the fixed point properties of right-angled Artin groups.

High performance matrix inversion techniques, such as the advanced order method (AOM) and its generalized variants (GeAOM), are specifically designed for GPU acceleration. These methods rely on a recursive decomposition of the matrix to be inverted, enabling linear complexity with respect to the matrix dimension. This paper introduces a novel approach termed "super order" (SO), which generalizes both AOM and GeAOM. We demonstrate that the SO method achieves inversion speeds comparable to CULA, a highly optimized library for GPU-accelerated matrix inversion. Furthermore, we establish that SO can surpass CULA's performance when inverting large sparse matrices. In addition to the new SO technique, we introduce a hybrid inversion algorithm that combines SO with direct inversion methods. Our results indicate that this hybrid approach is significantly faster than the SO method alone. Finally, we present a comprehensive generalization of the SO method, termed GE-SO, which extends the hybrid algorithm's capabilities. Numerical examples are provided to validate the efficacy of the generalized GE-SO method. The source code for all algorithms discussed in this study is available at https://github.com/ahmedshoukry/AdvancedOrderMatrixInversion.

Situational linear bandits represent a recently introduced framework designed to model non-stationary contextual bandits, where the context is defined by a tuple of variables: the current situation and the action taken. This model is particularly relevant for real-time decision-making systems, such as automated driving, where the situation encompasses environmental factors like weather, traffic, and road conditions, while the action refers to the vehicle's maneuver. In this work, we investigate learning in distributed situational linear bandits under the constraint that agents operate without access to the contextual definition. Specifically, we consider a setup where a learner interacts with K distinct environments through M situations, with each environment managed by a distinct agent. We demonstrate that if the environments are fully observable, the learner can achieve a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{dNM\log(K)})$. Conversely, for partially observable environments, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{dNM\log(K)})$, indicating that this bound is optimal up to constant factors. To address partially observable scenarios, we propose a novel algorithm that nearly matches this lower bound. Finally, we validate our approach using a real-world dataset. Our findings reveal that, in situations where the contextual definition is unknown, the learner can still learn effectively in partially observable environments, provided the environments are homogeneous. However, in heterogeneous environments, the regret grows linearly with the number of environments, rendering learning infeasible. This result underscores the critical importance of environment homogeneity when the contextual definition remains inaccessible.

We conducted global 3D hydrodynamic simulations to examine how dust development influences the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Our findings indicate that the VSI generates turbulent motions capable of driving rapid dust settling, which in turn amplifies local dust densities and enhances radiative cooling. This positive feedback loop accelerates VSI activity and increases turbulent velocities. However, once dust concentration reaches a certain threshold, the VSI is suppressed by the resulting rise in gas temperature. Simulations utilizing a standard cooling timescale ($\tau_{\rm cool} = 10\Omega^{-1}$) show that dust layers can settle to approximately $H_{\rm dust} \sim 0.01$, with turbulent velocities in the midplane exceeding $v_{\rm turb} \sim 100\rm\,m\,s^{-1}$. These conditions are conducive to the formation of pebble-sized particles. Furthermore, simulations with longer cooling timescales ($\tau_{\rm cool} \ge 20\Omega^{-1}$) reveal that dust accumulation can further intensify cooling, potentially leading to dust-induced gravitational instability in the disk's outer regions. These results suggest that the positive feedback between dust settling and VSI activation can accelerate dust growth and potentially trigger dust-driven gravitational instability in protoplanetary disks. Such mechanisms may help explain the high dust-to-gas ratios and gas depletion observed in the external regions of these disks. Our simulations also demonstrate that VSI-driven turbulent motions can sustain dust layers at $H_{\rm dust} \sim 0.01$ even when the gas scale height is $H_{\rm gas} \sim 0.03$, a scenario where hydrostatic equilibrium alone would cause the dust to settle deeper. Consequently, VSI-induced turbulence offers a viable mechanism for maintaining dust layers at altitudes higher than those predicted by hydrostatic balance, which is significant for understanding dust settling and the formation of dust gaps in protoplanetary disks. This work examines harmonic functions defined on Ricci diminutives that possess a non-negative sectional curvature and maintain a constant scalar curvature. We establish a Liouville theorem for such manifolds and demonstrate its application to derive a rigidity result for the Cheeger-Gromoll splitting theorem. Additionally, we utilize this theorem to prove that the fundamental group of a complete Riemannian manifold with non-negative sectional curvature and an isoperimetric doubling condition satisfies the Atiyah conjecture. The paper concludes with an exploration of the potential for further applications of the Liouville theorem. The central argument relies on a Bochner formula, which is derived through a novel approach. Furthermore, we introduce a new comparison lemma for the Hessian of the B-Yau function, which serves as the key component in proving the Liouville theorem. This lemma also enables the derivation of a Laplacian comparison for the B-Yau function, which in turn facilitates the proof of a gradient estimate for harmonic functions. Ultimately, this gradient estimate is employed to establish the Liouville theorem itself.

This work introduces a dynamic entrance layer that substitutes the conventional initial weight matrix in fully connected layers, embedding layers, and transformers. By integrating global mean pooling, the layer generates embedding vectors from input features, which are then projected onto a fixed-dimensional embedding space via a weight matrix. We demonstrate that this module can be seamlessly incorporated into existing models without altering their architecture. Extensive experiments across various tasks and models confirm that this simple addition consistently enhances performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rohitgupta007/GlobalMeanPooling.

This work introduces Random Stroll for Education (RfE), a novel approach to Federated Learning (FL) designed to enhance model performance on data from underrepresented clients. By integrating a random walk algorithm with gradient descent, RfE enables clients with limited data to leverage information from other participants. We evaluated RfE against standard FL and data sharing methods using a real-world dataset from an Indian school district. The results demonstrate that RfE significantly outperforms both baseline approaches, particularly for schools with small datasets. Furthermore, the method exhibits strong scalability, showing minimal performance degradation as dataset sizes increase. These findings suggest that Random Stroll for Education can effectively bridge data gaps in Federated Learning, offering a viable solution for data scarcity in educational contexts. The code is available at https://github.com/Anushree-1999/RfE.

This work introduces an uncomplicated consistency regularization method designed to enhance the performance of fully convolutional networks in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The approach leverages both labeled and unlabeled data by training the model on the labeled set and generating predictions for the unlabeled images. These predictions are then utilized as pseudo-labels to create consistency regularization terms, which are incorporated into the loss function alongside the segmentation loss derived from the labeled data. The model is optimized using a combination of segmentation and consistency regularization losses. Extensive experiments were conducted on three public datasets: ACDC, Pancreas, and BraTS. Results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques across all three datasets. Furthermore, the approach exhibits strong robustness against noisy labels, a common challenge in real-world scenarios. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Basic-Consistency-Regulization.

Genuine nonlocal phenomena, such as steering and nonlocal hidden variable models requiring global wavefunction collapse, are typically demonstrated using entangled multi-particle states. In this work, we introduce a protocol for genuine nonlocal effects based on single-particle entanglement, where a remote observer steers a superposition of a photon's presence in two spatially separated modes. This steering occurs through a combination of local operations and nonlocal guidance, the latter arising from the dependence of the wavefunction's shape on local measurement outcomes. We validate this protocol experimentally by generating nonlocal quantum correlations. Furthermore, we establish genuine nonlocal correlations via a Bell inequality that incorporates nonlocal guidance, which are violated using a steering inequality. These findings indicate that nonlocal guidance is an intrinsic feature of quantum mechanics, analogous to nonlocal collapse. Consequently, single-particle entanglement enables genuine nonlocal effects, offering a novel resource for quantum information processing tasks.

Long-term video identification systems are computationally intensive, making it difficult to deploy deep learning models on resource-constrained hardware. Although LSTM networks are effective for long-term video identification, their high computational demands hinder implementation on embedded systems. This paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-development approach to create energy-efficient LSTM networks using a fully connected hierarchical Tucker decomposition (HTD) framework. We propose a novel HTD-based LSTM architecture and develop a corresponding hardware design. To optimize the hardware, we introduce a memory sharing strategy that minimizes storage requirements. Furthermore, we designed a lightweight, high-performance HTD-LSTM network with 100 time steps for video identification tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our optimized HTD-LSTM architecture achieves a 99.9% identification accuracy, comparable to a standard LSTM with 100 time steps, while reducing energy consumption by 90.7% and area by 70.7%. Additionally, the hardware design for the optimized HTD-LSTM consumes 50.7% less energy and occupies 50.7% less area than a design based on a lightweight state-of-the-art model. The proposed architecture and hardware design are implemented on an FPGA, and the hardware design is available for download at: http://www.ee.cuhk.edu.hk/\textasciitilde liuzhiliang/HTD-LSTM.

This work examines the relationship between the primality of the focus and the iterates of the composition of polynomial pairs. It also investigates the connection between the primality of the focus and the iterates of the pair of compositions of polynomials. Finally, the study explores the link between the primality of the focus and the iterates of the pair of combinations of polynomial pairs.

This study examines the Schr\"odinger equation defined on the exterior of a convex barrier, subject to nonlinear Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the solution blows up in finite time when the initial data is sufficiently concentrated and possesses negative energy. Furthermore, we establish that the solution remains confined within a ball of radius $R(t)$, where $R(t)$ approaches zero as $t$ nears the blow-up moment. These findings extend earlier work by Merle and Zaag \cite{MZ} on the Schr\"odinger equation in $\mathbb{R}^n$ without boundary conditions, as well as research by Agueh, Gondran, and Jabin \cite{AGJ} on the heat equation in the same domain. The analysis relies on a comparison principle and a trapping argument.

This work introduces a non-deterministic semi-parametric local-characteristic algorithm designed to construct local-characteristic finite-state automaton abbreviations for varieties defined within a specific semi-parametric context. The algorithm operates under the assumption that a deterministic context grammar (either parametric or local in nature) for the variety is available. It is demonstrated that, within a specified context, a finite-state automaton abbreviation for a variety can be converted into a deterministic context grammar (either local or parametric) for that same variety. Furthermore, it is proven that if the initial context is both positive-characteristic and local, then the resulting final context will also be local and positive-characteristic. Finally, the combination of the non-deterministic semi-parametric local-characteristic algorithm for creating local-characteristic finite-state automaton abbreviations and the two deterministic semi-parametric local-characteristic algorithms for converting these abbreviations into local-characteristic context grammars yields a novel non-deterministic semi-parametric local-characteristic algorithm. This new algorithm can decide the emptiness problem for specific varieties in a given local-characteristic context, provided their context grammar is deterministic and local within that context. The significance of these findings lies in the demonstration that, under specific contexts, varieties over finitely presented $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras can be abbreviated into finite-state automata in positive-characteristic local contexts, and subsequently, these abbreviations can be transformed into context grammars in the same contexts. These results hold particular importance for varieties associated with Diophantine problems. To support these algorithms, a collection of supporting lemmas and theorems regarding formal languages, automata, and grammars in local-characteristic contexts is also presented. All algorithms and proofs are developed within the framework of constructive mathematics. The source code for these algorithms is accessible at https://github.com/ConstructiveMathematics/Local-Characteristic-Context-Varieties. Constructively, it is established that for any specific variety, there exists a constructive method to determine whether it admits a deterministic context grammar in a given local-characteristic context. Additionally, constructive algorithms exist for generating a finite set of test varieties in a specific local-characteristic context, which can be used to verify if a variety's context grammar accepts a particular formal language. By applying these algorithms, it was verified in characteristic three that the variety of commutative monoids defined by the set of Fibonacci Diophantine expressions over the standard signature does not possess a deterministic monoid grammar in that context. This study introduces a workflow for conducting Bayesian analyses using the R package BfCore, which integrates the R2WinBUGS interface to OpenBUGS and JAGS. The workflow comprises three sequential phases: first, researchers specify the scientific question and select appropriate models; second, they evaluate the evidence for the target hypothesis by examining posterior distributions of Bayes factors; and finally, they interpret the results through the lens of prior expectations regarding Bayes factors. The authors demonstrate this workflow with two examples: a replication of the famous "Bob's coin toss" scenario and an analysis of the data from the Nisbett and Borgida (1975) study on stereotyping. The resulting report offers a comprehensive summary of the study's objectives, data, model specifications, findings, and interpretations. By following this structured approach, researchers can produce detailed, transparent reports that fully articulate the goals, methods, and conclusions of their Bayesian studies. The R/BfCore workflow and its corresponding report are accessible at http://cran.r-project.org/package=BfCore.

Discourse indicators, which signal linguistic relationships between sentences, are essential for ensuring textual coherence. While prior research has primarily relied on manual methods to identify and classify these indicators, this work introduces a fully automated approach for detection and classification. We introduce a high-quality, gold-standard dataset comprising over 100,000 instances of 19 distinct discourse indicators across 11 categories, drawn from the Wikipedia abstracts of 1,999 articles. This dataset, named DiscSense, is made publicly available. Utilizing this data, we trained and evaluated three state-of-the-art neural models for joint detection and classification. Our results indicate that the contextualized transformer model, XLM-RoBERTa, surpasses all previous methods on our dataset. Furthermore, our analyses offer valuable insights into the characteristics of discourse indicators, their distribution within texts, and the specific challenges associated with each indicator. The accompanying code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/linguamatics/DiscSense.

This paper introduces a family of Jordanian twists derived from the universal $R$-matrix of the negative Borel subalgebra of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. These twists generate a deformation of the Lie algebra brace structure on the associated Hopf algebra. By utilizing the explicit formula for the Jordanian twist, we demonstrate that the corresponding deformed Lie algebra brace yields a modified $q$-brace structure. Furthermore, we establish that the Jordanian twisted $q$-brace aligns with the $q$-brace structure arising from the Drinfeld twist of the same subalgebra within the Drinfeld double of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Finally, we apply the Jordanian twisted coproduct to construct deformed vertex operators for the negative Borel subalgebra of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. These operators facilitate the definition of highest weight modules for the Jordanian twisted Borel subalgebra, which are subsequently employed to generate intertwining operators for the $q$-brace. Ultimately, we utilize the Jordanian twist to derive an explicit formulation of the Drinfeld twist for the Borel subalgebra of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm for resolving syntactic inequalities between extended regular expressions (ERREs), which include the Kleene star, complement, and boolean operators. The proposed method combines a symbolic approach with a resolution-based strategy, utilizing a decision procedure for ERREs to transform resolution steps into a purely symbolic process. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a collection of challenging examples, including the verification of inclusions between complex ERREs and the extraction of explicit regular expressions that satisfy syntactic inequalities. Furthermore, we integrate this algorithm into the Aho tool, a suite of utilities for manipulating and analyzing regular expressions. Empirical results indicate that the enhanced Aho tool, now equipped with this resolution algorithm, can solve instances of ERRE inclusions and other related problems that were previously unsolvable. The algorithm is described in detail, its correctness is formally proven, and its complexity is analyzed. Finally, the work presents a collection of examples illustrating the application of the symbolic resolution of ERRE inequalities to various domains. The source code and additional materials are accessible at https://github.com/ahotools/symbolic-resolution.

In the context of AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$, we examine the AdS$_{3}$ action associated with a specific OPE segment, defined as the geodesic connecting the insertion points of two primary fields. By utilizing the AdS$_{3}$ bulk action, we derive a closed-form expression for the OPE segment action. Subsequently, we analyze the dependence of this action on the conformal dimension of the primary fields and their separation. Our results align with expectations derived from the CFT$_{2}$ action. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the action of a rotating OPE segment can be decomposed into the actions of two non-rotating segments. Finally, we apply these findings to the study of AdS$_{3}$ geodesic loops.

We introduce a novel architecture for lobster-eye X-ray telescopes designed to enable broad-field monitoring with high temporal resolution. This configuration utilizes multiple lobster-eye lenses, each paired with a conventional focusing telescope to create a multiplexed system capable of achieving high spectral resolution within a wide field of view. We present a simulation of this setup aimed at detecting X-ray transients in the vicinity of neutron stars and black holes. The findings indicate that this design can detect and precisely localize X-ray flares from accretion disks, thereby offering a powerful tool for identifying transient events and identifying new X-ray binaries. Furthermore, the system would facilitate the rapid identification of optical counterparts for X-ray transients, potentially enabling the discovery of tidal disruption events. The multiplexed lobster-eye architecture represents a cost-effective solution for broad-field monitoring that could complement existing and future X-ray telescopes, such as IXPE, RXTI, and the NEO-Sat, to advance our understanding of variable compact X-ray sources. A demonstration of this concept is currently being constructed at the NSF/SLAC LUXE beamline.

We introduce a novel deep learning framework to investigate the role of the cosmic speed field in determining dark matter halo mass distribution. Utilizing the large-scale simulation TNG300, we trained a ResNet-50 model to predict halo mass from dark matter phase-space information, specifically density and velocity. The resulting predictions align closely with TNG300 data, yielding a mean absolute error of 0.031 in logarithmic mass. Our analysis reveals that the model implicitly learns the halo mass–concentration relation and incorporates the influence of tidal truncation on mass growth. Furthermore, we examined how both density and velocity individually contribute to mass determination, finding that the halo mass–concentration relation primarily drives the impact of density, while tidal truncation governs the velocity's contribution. Finally, we explored the relative significance of density versus velocity across different mass ranges and cosmic epochs, concluding that density is the dominant factor for low-mass halos, whereas velocity becomes more influential for high-mass halos at late times. These results offer new insights into the physical mechanisms governing dark matter halo mass assembly. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/CosmicSpeedField.

We demonstrate that atomic interferometry can detect local magnetic field changes via the Meissner effect in superconductors, enabling detection of field alterations too localized to influence the interferometer's arms directly. Using this setup, we measured local magnetic field variations with a sensitivity of 0.11 nT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ over a 10-second integration period. This sensitivity surpasses the best previously reported sensitivity for local field detection by a factor of 10. The observed sensitivity aligns with a lower bound determined by the local field fluctuations inherent in the bulk superconductor. This technique offers a promising method for identifying local magnetic anomalies in materials, which could aid in the search for hidden magnetic moments in nominally non-magnetic substances. Furthermore, it serves as a valuable tool for characterizing local magnetic field fluctuations in superconducting materials. The experimental arrangement is straightforward and potentially adaptable to various atomic interferometers and superconductors. The described method represents a significant advancement in the sensitivity of local magnetic field detection through atomic interferometry. Previously, such detection relied on magnetometers, which are limited by the difficulty of measuring field changes in regions with no initial field. In contrast, atomic interferometers can sense local field variations regardless of the background field strength. By leveraging the superconductor's global magnetic response, we were able to observe local field fluctuations without requiring active shielding. This approach could be extended to other materials exhibiting global magnetic responses, such as ferromagnets, to detect local field alterations. Additionally, this technique could be applied to detect local gravitational field variations, potentially surpassing the sensitivity of current gravitational sensors. Such an application would be particularly useful for investigating local gravitational anomalies in materials with strong gravitational responses, including neutron stars. Ultimately, this method could contribute to testing theories of quantum gravity. This study employs the relativistic initial principles theory to investigate magnetic Y--Rusinov (Yu--RS) states formed by an Mn adatom and various Mn dimer configurations on the Nb(110) surface. The analysis focuses on the spinor wave function, spin density, spin texture, and spin texture lines associated with both the ground state and excited states of the Yu--RS. Results indicate that the spin texture lines for the ground state align with the magnetic anisotropy axes, whereas those of the excited states correspond to the anisotropy axes of the excited states themselves. Furthermore, the spin texture lines of the ground state for the antiferromagnetic (AFM) and ferromagnetic (FM) dimers match those of the AFM and FM excited states, respectively, of the corresponding adatom. These findings suggest that the spin texture lines of Yu--RS states on an fcc(111) Fe monolayer with a vacuum overlayer, as reported by Zhang et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 110, 127201 (2013)), can similarly be utilized to determine magnetic anisotropy axes. Additionally, the relativistic initial principles theory offers a straightforward method for calculating spin texture lines, which can serve as a valuable tool for analyzing spin textures in other systems. The initial principles theory, along with its extension to the relativistic initial principles theory, is detailed in Appendix A.

Skin cancer remains a significant global health challenge, with nonmelanoma skin carcinomas (NMSC) being the most prevalent form. The scarcity of labeled NMSC images represents a major obstacle to developing effective detection systems. This study introduces a novel framework for identifying NMSC using a combination of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and an outlier detection mechanism. We evaluated our approach on the first publicly available dataset of nonmelanoma skin carcinomas, which includes images categorized into five distinct subtypes. Our method involves training a CNN on four of the subtypes to generate feature vectors, which are then analyzed by an outlier detection algorithm to identify the fifth subtype. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework successfully classified the unseen subtype with an accuracy of 98.1%. Furthermore, the system effectively identified outlier samples across all five subtypes, as confirmed by both quantitative metrics and visual analysis. These findings indicate that the proposed framework can accurately detect the specific subtype of nonmelanoma skin carcinoma and flag potential outliers within each category that may require further investigation. The dataset is accessible at: http://nmsc-skin-cancer-dataset.kit.edu/. The source code for this work can be found at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/NMSC-Identification-Using-CNN-and-Outlier-Detection. Keywords: Nonmelanoma skin carcinoma, Convolutional neural network, Outlier detection, Image classification.

This study introduces a rapid, event-by-event method for calculating the $q^2$ dependence of lepton universality ratios in forward muon interactions. The approach relies on a simplified model of $W$-boson polarization, which is justified by the high energies characteristic of fixed-target experiments. The technique is validated against Monte Carlo simulations of $\nu_\mu$ interactions generated by the NuWro and GiBUU models, demonstrating excellent agreement. Furthermore, the method's performance is evaluated using real data from the SeaXray experiment. The resulting $q^2$-dependent lepton universality ratios align well with data from the LEP and SLD colliders, provided that the $q^2$ ranges are comparable. Finally, the utility of this method for analyzing future high-intensity muon beam experiments is discussed. The implementation is accessible via the open-source NuMuUli toolkit at https://github.com/SeaXray/NuMuUli.

This section of the paper presents a proof of Theorem 1.1, which asserts that the collection of theories $T$ satisfying $Con(PA) \vdash Con(T)$ and $PA \cup T \vdash Con(PA)$ is not closed under finite extensions. The proof relies on the work of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. Specifically, Godel's first and second incompleteness theorems are formalized as $I1(T)$ and $I2(T)$, respectively. Tarski's undefinability theorem is expressed as $U1(T)$, while Carnap's and Rosser's results are denoted by $C(T)$ and $R(T)$. The central argument utilizes a hierarchy of diagonalization lemmas, labeled $D_n(T)$, which are derived from $I1(T)$, $U1(T)$, $C(T)$, and $R(T)$. These lemmas are then employed to establish Theorem 1.1. Readers interested in the detailed definitions and derivations of $I1(T)$, $I2(T)$, $U1(T)$, $C(T)$, $R(T)$, and $D_n(T)$ are directed to Section 2. The proof of Theorem 1.1 itself is provided in Section 3.

Invariant surfaces play a crucial role in the analysis of dynamical systems, particularly in reducing dimensionality and facilitating the study of complex behaviors like chaos. This work examines invariant surfaces for a specific class of three-dimensional systems known as fractional-order Liénard systems. We demonstrate that, contrary to the integer-order case, no such invariant surfaces exist for these fractional-order systems. Consequently, the standard approach for investigating chaos in fractional-order Liénard systems—relying on the Poincaré-Bendixson Theorem and invariant surfaces—is fundamentally flawed. To address this, we propose an alternative method for analyzing chaotic dynamics in these systems. As a practical application, we identify chaotic attractors in a fractional-order extension of the Chua circuit. Furthermore, we introduce a novel chaos measure based on Lyapunov exponents to quantify chaotic behavior, offering a useful tool for future research. Finally, we validate the existence of these attractors through numerical simulations.

This study addresses the inverse challenge of a structural acoustic engagement, aiming to reconstruct the characteristics of an unknown acoustic excitation acting on a structure. The reconstruction relies on the structure's response, measured via an optical full-field technique, and its boundary conditions. The excitation is modeled as a combination of a deterministic component and a stochastic component, with the latter represented by a finite sum of stochastic processes. The deterministic part is reconstructed using a sparse regularization approach, while the stochastic component is characterized through its spectral density function. The overall reconstruction problem is solved iteratively by alternating between updating the deterministic and stochastic components. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated using a simply supported plate subjected to an unknown excitation composed of a deterministic signal and white noise. Results indicate that the approach successfully reconstructs both the deterministic signal and the spectral density function of the excitation. Furthermore, the study analyzes the impact of regularization parameters and the number of stochastic processes on reconstruction quality. Finally, a potential application of this method in identifying structural acoustic excitations is discussed.

We present the minimal extension of the simplest "seesaw of seesaws" framework required to achieve a vacuum robustness comparable to the standard model (SM) and enable direct detection of dark matter (DM) via $t$-channel scattering. Within this model, the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP)-like DM is identified as the lightest neutral scalar, while the dominant $t$-channel scattering amplitude arises from tree-level exchanges of heavy right-handed neutrinos. We perform a comprehensive phenomenological analysis, determining the viable parameter space that satisfies all theoretical and experimental constraints. Our study includes a detailed examination of the leading DM direct detection signatures, the characteristics of new physics at colliders, and the model's testability at future colliders. We also analyze the hierarchy among the three neutrino mass scales and the masses of the new particles. To guide the search for dark matter at direct detection experiments, we calculated the median expected significance for identifying scalar DM within the allowed parameter space across various exposure levels. Our findings indicate that for the minimal viable parameter space, the significance of detecting DM at a 95\% confidence level at a future 10-year SuperLHC (sLHC) with a 0.5\tonne exposure would range between $1.5\sigma$ and $2.5\sigma$, contingent upon the specific mass configurations. Furthermore, we determined the optimal parameter space for maximizing the production of new particles at a 100\textquotedblleft$\,$ TeV$ $ collider and for achieving the highest possible DM direct detection signals. The complete theoretical and phenomenological details, including a thorough discussion of theoretical constraints, are provided in the main text and two accompanying appendices, with all results visualized through extensive plots. The simplest version of this framework, featuring a dark matter mass of $m_{\rm
  DM}=10$\,GeV, is accessible for simulation via the public code available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/EasiestScotoSeesaw. Ultimately, we anticipate that the future 100\textquotedblleft$,\, $ TeV$ $ collider will be essential for exploring the remaining unexplored regions of the parameter space. This work serves as a foundational study, and we intend to investigate the phenomenology of non-minimal extensions in our forthcoming research.
